We used CaG WGS to compare different approaches to study VCI in the gene SPG7 (MIM 602783). PathogenicvariantsinSPG7areassociatedwithanautosomalrecessive form of hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP, MIM 607259) that is characterized by adult-onset progressive bilateral leg weakness and spasticity, sensory neuropathy, and in some cases ataxia and dysarthria38.Diagnosisisbasedontypicalclinicalfindingsandidenti-

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this study, authors presents the Quebec Reference Genome Panel (QGP), a newly developed whole-genome sequencing
(WGS) reference panel based on a multi-ancestry cohort of ~30k individuals from the CARTaGENE biobank (30k for GWAS
genotyping and 3k for WGS). The QGP reflects the genetic diversity within Quebec, a Canadian province with complex
demographic history shaped by French colonial founders, British settlers, and recent immigrants. The panel improves
genetic imputation accuracy across ancestries, especially for low-frequency and population-specific variants, HLA variants,
and includes annotated data on rare coding variants and their geographic distributions. GWAS results for the set of the
phenotypes were presented. This resource serves as a critical tool for precision health research in Quebec and globally,
while acknowledging the importance of inclusivity in genetic references. This is a well-presented manuscript for the
population- and region-specific cohorts.
1. Population demography of the cohort looks interesting. This reviewer is interested in more locus-specific story on the
target population, derived from the genome-wide natural selection screening.
2. HLA genotype calling based on WGS is still methodologically under development and lacks accuracy. Validation of the
called HLA variants using other typing methods is recommended. Calling of non-classical HLA genes such as HLA-E/F/G is
generally still challenging, and as far as this reviewer knows, WGS-based calling is not accurate to date.
3. Overview of the GWAS design and results (No. phenotypes for each category, No. identified loci) can better to be
presented in the main Figure.
4. As always, there exist discussions on multiple comparisons of GWAS significance based on the No. phenotypes. This
reviewer does not request to strictly apply the threshold considering the multiple comparison burden, but it would be better to
indicate how the number of the significant loci would change after application.
5. The value of the manuscript depends on data availability. Current statement ‘The CaG genetic and phenotypid data is
available from … after scientific and ethical review’ may not satisfy the Nature journal data deposit request. Direct deposit of
the data to public resources such as dbGAP or EGA would be necessary.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have performed a very detailed and interesting study on explorative genetic insights of the Quebec region
population in Canada and identification of novel genetic variants (basis sequencing associated imputation) with multiple
health outcomes.
I have some comments on the manuscript draft as follows:
1. Abstract: The authors mention about including 2173 CaG participants for sequencing followed by special mention of two
non-European populations. It would be good if the authors can mention the overall ethnic groups covered in their study
(genotyping and sequencing) eg. (Europeans %, Non-Europeans % (African/Morroco/Haiti, Asians etc.)).
2. Abstract: The authors have highlighted that they analyzed genes for rich phenotype and environmental data. Following
this they mention that they interpret variants of clinical importance followed by a mention how this is methodologically
advanced. It seems like a new database has been created through this study for future research use (eg. Quebec Genomics
Health db).
However, no key results have been mentioned in the abstract. A mention of the key findings: number and type of traits
analyzed (any top findings: monogenic or complex traits), accuracy and/or coverage of sequencing based imputation
compared to existing reference panels/previous studies on this population and/or how many new variants were identified
and if the focus was ona any specific population, would send out a clear message of the study strengths/novelty.
In the last sentence it is unclear if all this data is available for global or local research use? Is it the existing CaG study
database available for access or an extension to the current dataset (https://cartagene.qc.ca/en/researchers/genetic-
data.html)?
3. Methods/Results: Supplementary table 1: Include details of all participants studied (n=29337). Currently the ancistry-wise
% does not match the total number studied (19,342 (QFC + QHA + QMO)). Mention acronyms QHA and QMO in the Supp
table 1 as in main text. Similarly for the Whole genome sequenced CaG subset column. In case the authors studied only the
subset (QFC, QHA, and QMO) it needs to be speciied under methods section.
4. Methods:
a. Genotyping methods should mention some details of the quality control on GSA array data.
b. The authors mention about genotyping performed from 5 different projects: Do they mean different projects or batches?
Also if these were in regard to differing ethnic groups? Provide more details and if possible a flow chart showing steps
through the genotyping.
c. Also clearly define the MAF thresholds and variants filtered after genotyping (relevant for the five different projects/batches
and/or for the overall merged dataset).
5. Methods: WGS Data QC and Supp Table 2: The authors have mentioned biallelic SNVs and indels and corresponding
numbers in the main text that do not match the numbers in Supp table 2. Kindly check again, correct and use same
label/name for these in both places for ease of the reader (eg. SNV or "biallelic SNV" in both places).
6. Genetic structure in CaG (Supp Figure 1A and B): The authors have nicely conducted a PC analyses but a clear
composition of subcluseters (1-14) needs to be mentioned (possibly in tabular form) clearly highlighting the differences
between clusters.
7. Results (Ancestry form Americas): IS the CartaGene a representative population for the entire Quebec as it mostly covers
regions from the southern Quebec region. This needs to be mentioned. Compared to the original Quebec population
comprising
French, Canadian (overlapping with French), British, Indigenous, Other European and Non-European population needs to
be discussed in regard to the current study population. Also a chart as per timeline when these populations originated in
Quebec could be a good overall demonstration of the Quebec population with a highlight of what is covered by the current
study (sample collection centers). This will provide a clear image of the studied population at present time, which might be
predominant at some time point in history.
8. The study highlights enriched genetic variants in this population relating metabolic outcomes. The authors should
highlight this in the abstract. In case there is information on other health outcomes, such as diabetes, cardiovascular
disease, obesity etc. is available in CaG, their prevalence could be mentioned in a supplementary table making this dataset
comparable to other similar large datasets mentioned by the authors.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank both Reviewers for their insightful comments. We provide below a point-by-point
response to the questions that were raised. When appropriate, we also revised the
manuscript, with edits marked with blue font and new display items.
Reviewer #1:
1.1) Population demography of the cohort looks interesting. This reviewer is
interested in more locus-specific story on the target population, derived from the
genome-wide natural selection screening.
Response: We agree with the Reviewer that this would be interesting, but probably
better left for a future study. Identifying outlier variants would be doable, but we
believe that the interpretation of the results would be best accomplished in a
separate publication that would focus on natural selection in the Quebec population.
1.2) HLA genotype calling based on WGS is still methodologically under development
and lacks accuracy. Validation of the called HLA variants using other typing
methods is recommended. Calling of non-classical HLA genes such as HLA-
E/F/G is generally still challenging, and as far as this reviewer knows, WGS-based
calling is not accurate to date.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this limitation in our analyses. We
agree that short-read sequencing technology, even at >30X whole genome coverage
as used in our study, has limitations in accurately resolving HLA haplotypes, and it is
not suitable for clinical applications or for detecting ultra-rare genetic variants.
However, using high-depth WGS data for HLA calling and imputation in population-
based biobanks is widely accepted, as demonstrated in studies such as PMID:
34611364 (HLA calling from WGS), PMID: 37923823 (HLA calling from WES), and
PMID: 35221124 (HLA imputation). In our analyses, we used HLA-LA (PMID:
30942877) for calling, which is well-established and was thoroughly evaluated in its
 its
original manuscript and independent works (e.g., PMID: 36426357, PMID: 37161318)
and is considered one of the most accurate HLA callers available; the authors report
99.4% accuracy from whole-genome sequencing data. To minimize false positives as
much as possible, we performed the following: (1) we applied the most strict
thresholds on HLA-LA’s documented quality metrics; (2) we compared the WGS-
based HLA alleles frequencies against their frequencies in Hema-Quebec donor
database to eliminate any outlier HLA allele with discordant frequency; (3) as the
reviewer noted, the calling accuracy varies by HLA gene, and thus, we excluded from
our analyses alleles in genes HLA-DRB3 and -DRB4 that are known to be highly
problematic to call. Although non-classical genes (HLA-E, -F, -G) were not excluded
1
by these technical filters, they were not included in downstream analyses due to the
current lack of comparable frequency data and interoperability with the tools used.
We also acknowledge potential false negatives due to the HLA-LA software relying on
a pre-built population reference graph, which may lack alleles from our study
population.
We have added the following sentences to the Methods section to be explicit about
specific numbers of alleles used in analyses, and limitations of the HLA calling:
“We also removed HLA-E, -F, and -G alleles from the panel for downstream analyses
due to a lack of comparable allele frequencies and interoperability with
computational tools used. Thus, the final HLA WGS panel included 31,199 alleles in
2,088 samples. However, it is important to note that our HLA analyses are subject to
inherent limitations from short-read sequencing technology, which leads to lower
calling accuracy compared to SNVs. Furthermore, reference graph-based HLA calling
tools may miss certain HLA alleles that are absent from the reference.”
We also added the following sentence to the “HLA Genotyping” section in Results:
“We note that our HLA analyses are subject to the inherent limitations of calling HLA
alleles from short-read sequencing technology, which leads to lower calling accuracy
compared to SNVs."
“HLA-E, -F, and -G alleles passed quality thresholds but were not used in subsequent
analyses due to lack of comparative allele frequency data. ”
1.3) Overview of the GWAS design and results (No. phenotypes for each category, No.
identified loci) can better to be presented in the main Figure.
Response: We have created a new Supplementary Figure 18 to answer the
Reviewer’s question.
1.4) As always, there exist discussions on multiple comparisons of GWAS
significance based on the No. phenotypes. This reviewer does not request to
strictly apply the threshold considering the multiple comparison burden, but it
would be better to indicate how the number of the significant loci would change
after application.
Response: We used a standard P-value <5x10-8 threshold for our analysis, considering
that a single phenotype represents a separate “family” of tests, which aligns with the
common situation where researchers focus on just one phenotype. As the reviewer
suggested, we also adjusted our Bonferroni threshold to account for 42 different
phenotypes (i.e., 0.05 / (1,000,000 x 42)), reflecting a more exploratory approach to
identify associations across all traits. Although the number of loci decreased, we still
observed that the CaG reference panel and meta-imputation enhance the number of
2
genome-wide significant loci compared to imputation based only on TOPMed r3. We
added these numbers in Supplementary Table 15.

1.5) The value of the manuscript depends on data availability. Current statement ‘The
CaG genetic and phenotypid data is available from … after scientific and ethical
review’ may not satisfy the Nature journal data deposit request. Direct deposit of
the data to public resources such as dbGAP or EGA would be necessary.
Response: We apologize for the confusion. The CaG data is available for global use.
CaG has a very similar data access procedure as the UK Biobank. Investigators who
wish to access the data need to have local ethical approval and submit a project
application to the CaG data access committee. Projects are scientifically reviewed to
ensure that they align with CaG’s broad mission to advance biomedical research. The
data access procedure is detailed under the URL included in our DATA AVAILABILITY
STATEMENT: https://cartagene.qc.ca/en/researchers/access-request.html. For these
reasons, the CaG data cannot be submitted to dbGaP/EGA.
Reviewer #2:
2.1) Abstract: The authors mention about including 2173 CaG participants for
sequencing followed by special mention of two non-European populations. It
would be good if the authors can mention the overall ethnic groups covered in
their study (genotyping and sequencing) eg. (Europeans %, Non-Europeans %
(African/Morroco/Haiti, Asians etc.))
Response: We clarified in the abstract that CaG is a multi-ancestry cohort. The
genotyping component included all individuals who provided consent for DNA
analysis in the biobank, and as such have a wide diversity of ancestral profiles. This
has been clarified in the abstract, and details have been added in Figure 1 (we added
sample size for each cluster) and Supplementary Table 1. By contrast, sequencing
data has focused on individuals with four grandparents from one of three countries
(Canada, Morocco and Haiti).
2.2) Abstract: The authors have highlighted that they analyzed genes for rich
phenotype and environmental data. Following this they mention that they
interpret variants of clinical importance followed by a mention how this is
methodologically advanced. It seems like a new database has been created
through this study for future research use (eg. Quebec Genomics Health db).
However, no key results have been mentioned in the abstract. A mention of the
key findings: number and type of traits analyzed (any top findings: monogenic or
complex traits), accuracy and/or coverage of sequencing based imputation
compared to existing reference panels/previous studies on this population
and/or how many new variants were identified and if the focus was ona any
specific population, would send out a clear message of the study
strengths/novelty.
Response. The Reviewer is correct that this manuscript describes a new dataset
linked to data and a biobank, and this manuscript serves as an overall presentation
of the data and findings from a range of basic population and statistical genetic
analyses. Given the diversity of analyses presented, it is challenging to summarize all
the results within 200-words (word limit for the abstract). We did add the following
information in the revised abstract: (1) clarification that CaG is a multi-ancestry
cohort, (2) number of sequenced participants by ancestry, (3) mention that we used
SPG7 to illustrate the value of the CaG dataset to expand the study of rare diseases in
Quebec, (4) number of quantitative traits analyzed by GWAS (n=42 traits), and (5)
mention that imputation with the CaG panel increases the GWAS yield by ~7% when
compared to results generated with data imputed using the much larger TOPMed
imputation panel.

research use? Is it the existing CaG study database available for access or an
extension to the current dataset
(https://cartagene.qc.ca/en/researchers/genetic-data.html)?
Response: Data is available for research use globally. It is indeed an extension to the
current dataset. See also our response to Reviewer #1, Question 5 above. We have
edited the abstract accordingly.

The three specified groups (QFC, QHA and QMO) form the bulk of the WGS efforts.
Data for 123 additional individuals of European ancestry with grandparents born in

healthcare lists in predetemined regions in the South of Quebec. This led to regional
biases, as well as a bias against recruitment of participants from Canadian
Indigenous backgrounds, since they are covered by a different healthcare system. In
addition, we expect different forms of response biases (e.g., participation rates were
much higher in individuals with higher education levels). As a result, the cohort
cannot be taken as statistically representative. With these limitations in mind, its
participants are diverse and represent a range of ancestries, regional origins,
socioeconomic statuses, and environmental exposures.

participants with a range of ancestral backgrounds, CaG is not completely representative

### Reviewer 1

In this study, authors presents the Quebec Reference Genome Panel (QGP), a newly developed whole-genome sequencing
(WGS) reference panel based on a multi-ancestry cohort of ~30k individuals from the CARTaGENE biobank (30k for GWAS
genotyping and 3k for WGS). The QGP reflects the genetic diversity within Quebec, a Canadian province with complex
demographic history shaped by French colonial founders, British settlers, and recent immigrants. The panel improves
genetic imputation accuracy across ancestries, especially for low-frequency and population-specific variants, HLA variants,
and includes annotated data on rare coding variants and their geographic distributions. GWAS results for the set of the
phenotypes were presented. This resource serves as a critical tool for precision health research in Quebec and globally,
while acknowledging the importance of inclusivity in genetic references. This is a well-presented manuscript for the
population- and region-specific cohorts.
1. Population demography of the cohort looks interesting. This reviewer is interested in more locus-specific story on the
target population, derived from the genome-wide natural selection screening.
2. HLA genotype calling based on WGS is still methodologically under development and lacks accuracy. Validation of the
called HLA variants using other typing methods is recommended. Calling of non-classical HLA genes such as HLA-E/F/G is
generally still challenging, and as far as this reviewer knows, WGS-based calling is not accurate to date.
3. Overview of the GWAS design and results (No. phenotypes for each category, No. identified loci) can better to be
presented in the main Figure.
4. As always, there exist discussions on multiple comparisons of GWAS significance based on the No. phenotypes. This
reviewer does not request to strictly apply the threshold considering the multiple comparison burden, but it would be better to
indicate how the number of the significant loci would change after application.
5. The value of the manuscript depends on data availability. Current statement ‘The CaG genetic and phenotypid data is
available from … after scientific and ethical review’ may not satisfy the Nature journal data deposit request. Direct deposit of
the data to public resources such as dbGAP or EGA would be necessary.

### Reviewer 2

The authors have performed a very detailed and interesting study on explorative genetic insights of the Quebec region
population in Canada and identification of novel genetic variants (basis sequencing associated imputation) with multiple
health outcomes.
I have some comments on the manuscript draft as follows:
1. Abstract: The authors mention about including 2173 CaG participants for sequencing followed by special mention of two
non-European populations. It would be good if the authors can mention the overall ethnic groups covered in their study
(genotyping and sequencing) eg. (Europeans %, Non-Europeans % (African/Morroco/Haiti, Asians etc.)).
2. Abstract: The authors have highlighted that they analyzed genes for rich phenotype and environmental data. Following
this they mention that they interpret variants of clinical importance followed by a mention how this is methodologically
advanced. It seems like a new database has been created through this study for future research use (eg. Quebec Genomics
Health db).
However, no key results have been mentioned in the abstract. A mention of the key findings: number and type of traits
analyzed (any top findings: monogenic or complex traits), accuracy and/or coverage of sequencing based imputation
compared to existing reference panels/previous studies on this population and/or how many new variants were identified
and if the focus was ona any specific population, would send out a clear message of the study strengths/novelty.
In the last sentence it is unclear if all this data is available for global or local research use? Is it the existing CaG study
database available for access or an extension to the current dataset (https://cartagene.qc.ca/en/researchers/genetic-
data.html)?
3. Methods/Results: Supplementary table 1: Include details of all participants studied (n=29337). Currently the ancistry-wise
% does not match the total number studied (19,342 (QFC + QHA + QMO)). Mention acronyms QHA and QMO in the Supp
table 1 as in main text. Similarly for the Whole genome sequenced CaG subset column. In case the authors studied only the
subset (QFC, QHA, and QMO) it needs to be speciied under methods section.
4. Methods:
a. Genotyping methods should mention some details of the quality control on GSA array data.
b. The authors mention about genotyping performed from 5 different projects: Do they mean different projects or batches?
Also if these were in regard to differing ethnic groups? Provide more details and if possible a flow chart showing steps
through the genotyping.
c. Also clearly define the MAF thresholds and variants filtered after genotyping (relevant for the five different projects/batches
and/or for the overall merged dataset).
5. Methods: WGS Data QC and Supp Table 2: The authors have mentioned biallelic SNVs and indels and corresponding
numbers in the main text that do not match the numbers in Supp table 2. Kindly check again, correct and use same
label/name for these in both places for ease of the reader (eg. SNV or "biallelic SNV" in both places).
6. Genetic structure in CaG (Supp Figure 1A and B): The authors have nicely conducted a PC analyses but a clear
composition of subcluseters (1-14) needs to be mentioned (possibly in tabular form) clearly highlighting the differences
between clusters.
7. Results (Ancestry form Americas): IS the CartaGene a representative population for the entire Quebec as it mostly covers
regions from the southern Quebec region. This needs to be mentioned. Compared to the original Quebec population
comprising
French, Canadian (overlapping with French), British, Indigenous, Other European and Non-European population needs to
be discussed in regard to the current study population. Also a chart as per timeline when these populations originated in
Quebec could be a good overall demonstration of the Quebec population with a highlight of what is covered by the current
study (sample collection centers). This will provide a clear image of the studied population at present time, which might be
predominant at some time point in history.
8. The study highlights enriched genetic variants in this population relating metabolic outcomes. The authors should
highlight this in the abstract. In case there is information on other health outcomes, such as diabetes, cardiovascular
disease, obesity etc. is available in CaG, their prevalence could be mentioned in a supplementary table making this dataset
comparable to other similar large datasets mentioned by the authors.

## Authors' Response to Round 1

We thank both Reviewers for their insightful comments. We provide below a point-by-point
response to the questions that were raised. When appropriate, we also revised the
manuscript, with edits marked with blue font and new display items.
Reviewer #1:
1.1) Population demography of the cohort looks interesting. This reviewer is
interested in more locus-specific story on the target population, derived from the
genome-wide natural selection screening.
Response: We agree with the Reviewer that this would be interesting, but probably
better left for a future study. Identifying outlier variants would be doable, but we
believe that the interpretation of the results would be best accomplished in a
separate publication that would focus on natural selection in the Quebec population.
1.2) HLA genotype calling based on WGS is still methodologically under development
and lacks accuracy. Validation of the called HLA variants using other typing
methods is recommended. Calling of non-classical HLA genes such as HLA-
E/F/G is generally still challenging, and as far as this reviewer knows, WGS-based
calling is not accurate to date.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this limitation in our analyses. We
agree that short-read sequencing technology, even at >30X whole genome coverage
as used in our study, has limitations in accurately resolving HLA haplotypes, and it is
not suitable for clinical applications or for detecting ultra-rare genetic variants.
However, using high-depth WGS data for HLA calling and imputation in population-
based biobanks is widely accepted, as demonstrated in studies such as PMID:
34611364 (HLA calling from WGS), PMID: 37923823 (HLA calling from WES), and
PMID: 35221124 (HLA imputation). In our analyses, we used HLA-LA (PMID:
30942877) for calling, which is well-established and was thoroughly evaluated in its
 its
original manuscript and independent works (e.g., PMID: 36426357, PMID: 37161318)
and is considered one of the most accurate HLA callers available; the authors report
99.4% accuracy from whole-genome sequencing data. To minimize false positives as
much as possible, we performed the following: (1) we applied the most strict
thresholds on HLA-LA’s documented quality metrics; (2) we compared the WGS-
based HLA alleles frequencies against their frequencies in Hema-Quebec donor
database to eliminate any outlier HLA allele with discordant frequency; (3) as the
reviewer noted, the calling accuracy varies by HLA gene, and thus, we excluded from
our analyses alleles in genes HLA-DRB3 and -DRB4 that are known to be highly
problematic to call. Although non-classical genes (HLA-E, -F, -G) were not excluded
1
by these technical filters, they were not included in downstream analyses due to the
current lack of comparable frequency data and interoperability with the tools used.
We also acknowledge potential false negatives due to the HLA-LA software relying on
a pre-built population reference graph, which may lack alleles from our study
population.
We have added the following sentences to the Methods section to be explicit about
specific numbers of alleles used in analyses, and limitations of the HLA calling:
“We also removed HLA-E, -F, and -G alleles from the panel for downstream analyses
due to a lack of comparable allele frequencies and interoperability with
computational tools used. Thus, the final HLA WGS panel included 31,199 alleles in
2,088 samples. However, it is important to note that our HLA analyses are subject to
inherent limitations from short-read sequencing technology, which leads to lower
calling accuracy compared to SNVs. Furthermore, reference graph-based HLA calling
tools may miss certain HLA alleles that are absent from the reference.”
We also added the following sentence to the “HLA Genotyping” section in Results:
“We note that our HLA analyses are subject to the inherent limitations of calling HLA
alleles from short-read sequencing technology, which leads to lower calling accuracy
compared to SNVs."
“HLA-E, -F, and -G alleles passed quality thresholds but were not used in subsequent
analyses due to lack of comparative allele frequency data. ”

identified loci) can better to be presented in the main Figure.
Response: We have created a new Supplementary Figure 18 to answer the

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this study, authors presents the Quebec Reference Genome Panel (QGP), a newly developed whole-genome sequencing
(WGS) reference panel based on a multi-ancestry cohort of ~30k individuals from the CARTaGENE biobank (30k for GWAS
genotyping and 3k for WGS). The QGP reflects the genetic diversity within Quebec, a Canadian province with complex
demographic history shaped by French colonial founders, British settlers, and recent immigrants. The panel improves
genetic imputation accuracy across ancestries, especially for low-frequency and population-specific variants, HLA variants,
and includes annotated data on rare coding variants and their geographic distributions. GWAS results for the set of the
phenotypes were presented. This resource serves as a critical tool for precision health research in Quebec and globally,
while acknowledging the importance of inclusivity in genetic references. This is a well-presented manuscript for the
population- and region-specific cohorts.
1. Population demography of the cohort looks interesting. This reviewer is interested in more locus-specific story on the
target population, derived from the genome-wide natural selection screening.
2. HLA genotype calling based on WGS is still methodologically under development and lacks accuracy. Validation of the
called HLA variants using other typing methods is recommended. Calling of non-classical HLA genes such as HLA-E/F/G is
generally still challenging, and as far as this reviewer knows, WGS-based calling is not accurate to date.
3. Overview of the GWAS design and results (No. phenotypes for each category, No. identified loci) can better to be
presented in the main Figure.
4. As always, there exist discussions on multiple comparisons of GWAS significance based on the No. phenotypes. This
reviewer does not request to strictly apply the threshold considering the multiple comparison burden, but it would be better to
indicate how the number of the significant loci would change after application.
5. The value of the manuscript depends on data availability. Current statement ‘The CaG genetic and phenotypid data is
available from … after scientific and ethical review’ may not satisfy the Nature journal data deposit request. Direct deposit of
the data to public resources such as dbGAP or EGA would be necessary.

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

We thank both Reviewers for their insightful comments. We provide below a point-by-point
response to the questions that were raised. When appropriate, we also revised the
manuscript, with edits marked with blue font and new display items.
Reviewer #1:
1.1) Population demography of the cohort looks interesting. This reviewer is
interested in more locus-specific story on the target population, derived from the
genome-wide natural selection screening.
Response: We agree with the Reviewer that this would be interesting, but probably
better left for a future study. Identifying outlier variants would be doable, but we
believe that the interpretation of the results would be best accomplished in a
separate publication that would focus on natural selection in the Quebec population.
1.2) HLA genotype calling based on WGS is still methodologically under development
and lacks accuracy. Validation of the called HLA variants using other typing
methods is recommended. Calling of non-classical HLA genes such as HLA-
E/F/G is generally still challenging, and as far as this reviewer knows, WGS-based
calling is not accurate to date.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this limitation in our analyses. We
agree that short-read sequencing technology, even at >30X whole genome coverage
as used in our study, has limitations in accurately resolving HLA haplotypes, and it is
not suitable for clinical applications or for detecting ultra-rare genetic variants.
However, using high-depth WGS data for HLA calling and imputation in population-
based biobanks is widely accepted, as demonstrated in studies such as PMID:
34611364 (HLA calling from WGS), PMID: 37923823 (HLA calling from WES), and
PMID: 35221124 (HLA imputation). In our analyses, we used HLA-LA (PMID:
30942877) for calling, which is well-established and was thoroughly evaluated in its
 its
original manuscript and independent works (e.g., PMID: 36426357, PMID: 37161318)
and is considered one of the most accurate HLA callers available; the authors report
99.4% accuracy from whole-genome sequencing data. To minimize false positives as
much as possible, we performed the following: (1) we applied the most strict
thresholds on HLA-LA’s documented quality metrics; (2) we compared the WGS-
based HLA alleles frequencies against their frequencies in Hema-Quebec donor
database to eliminate any outlier HLA allele with discordant frequency; (3) as the
reviewer noted, the calling accuracy varies by HLA gene, and thus, we excluded from
our analyses alleles in genes HLA-DRB3 and -DRB4 that are known to be highly
problematic to call. Although non-classical genes (HLA-E, -F, -G) were not excluded
1
by these technical filters, they were not included in downstream analyses due to the
current lack of comparable frequency data and interoperability with the tools used.
We also acknowledge potential false negatives due to the HLA-LA software relying on
a pre-built population reference graph, which may lack alleles from our study
population.
We have added the following sentences to the Methods section to be explicit about
specific numbers of alleles used in analyses, and limitations of the HLA calling:
“We also removed HLA-E, -F, and -G alleles from the panel for downstream analyses
due to a lack of comparable allele frequencies and interoperability with
computational tools used. Thus, the final HLA WGS panel included 31,199 alleles in
2,088 samples. However, it is important to note that our HLA analyses are subject to
inherent limitations from short-read sequencing technology, which leads to lower
calling accuracy compared to SNVs. Furthermore, reference graph-based HLA calling
tools may miss certain HLA alleles that are absent from the reference.”
We also added the following sentence to the “HLA Genotyping” section in Results:
“We note that our HLA analyses are subject to the inherent limitations of calling HLA
alleles from short-read sequencing technology, which leads to lower calling accuracy
compared to SNVs."
“HLA-E, -F, and -G alleles passed quality thresholds but were not used in subsequent
analyses due to lack of comparative allele frequency data. ”

phenotype and environmental data. Following this they mention that they
interpret variants of clinical importance followed by a mention how this is
methodologically advanced. It seems like a new database has been created
through this study for future research use (eg. Quebec Genomics Health db).
However, no key results have been mentioned in the abstract. A mention of the
key findings: number and type of traits analyzed (any top findings: monogenic or
complex traits), accuracy and/or coverage of sequencing based imputation

and/or how many new variants were identified and if the focus was ona any

Response. The Reviewer is correct that this manuscript describes a new dataset
linked to data and a biobank, and this manuscript serves as an overall presentation
of the data and findings from a range of basic population and statistical genetic
analyses. Given the diversity of analyses presented, it is challenging to summarize all
the results within 200-words (word limit for the abstract). We did add the following
information in the revised abstract: (1) clarification that CaG is a multi-ancestry
cohort, (2) number of sequenced participants by ancestry, (3) mention that we used
SPG7 to illustrate the value of the CaG dataset to expand the study of rare diseases in
Quebec, (4) number of quantitative traits analyzed by GWAS (n=42 traits), and (5)
mention that imputation with the CaG panel increases the GWAS yield by ~7% when
compared to results generated with data imputed using the much larger TOPMed
imputation panel.

2.5) Methods:
a. Genotyping methods should mention some details of the quality control on
GSA array data.
Response: We have added the following paragraph to the Methods section: “We
genotyped the CaG participants separately in five different projects between 2017
and 2021, each time using a slightly different version of Illumina’s GSA arrays
(Supplementary Fig. 2). One of the subsets (2017) was enriched for restless leg
syndrome cases. The remaining sets were not ascertained for particular diseases
or ancestral groups. We used PLINK 1.9 to perform genotype data quality-control
in each batch separately (Supplementary Fig. 2). We removed samples with: (1)
low genotyping success rate (<95%), (2) sex mismatch with the database, (3)
duplicates based on IBD analyses, and (4) samples that share a fraction of their
genome with many (>50%) of the participants (i.e. contaminants). We excluded
variants with: (1) low genotyping success rate (<95%), (2) monomorphic or
duplicates, (3) Hardy-Weinberg P-value <1x10-6, (4) indels with unspecified alleles
(e.g. “D”, “I”), (5) Y-linked variants, and (6) variants with a large allele frequency
variance between the five batches (measured using the perpendicular distance to
the unity line). We also aligned all alleles on the positive strand
(https://www.well.ox.ac.uk/~wrayner/strand). We merged the datasets, keeping
only variants available to all five batches. We obtained a cleaned dataset of
29,337 participants and 472,467 variants.”
b. The authors mention about genotyping performed from 5 different projects:
Do they mean different projects or batches? Also if these were in regard to
differing ethnic groups? Provide more details and if possible a flow chart

enriched for restless leg syndrome cases, the genotyping project were not
ascertained for phenotypes nor ancestral groups.
c. Also clearly define the MAF thresholds and variants filtered after genotyping
(relevant for the five different projects/batches and/or for the overall merged
dataset).
otherwise did not explicitly filter out variants based on MAF. Because we only kept

2.8) Results (Ancestry form Americas): Is the CartaGene a representative population
for the entire Quebec as it mostly covers regions from the southern Quebec
region. This needs to be mentioned.
Response: The cohort was recruited by randomly contacting people from provincial
healthcare lists in predetemined regions in the South of Quebec. This led to regional
biases, as well as a bias against recruitment of participants from Canadian
Indigenous backgrounds, since they are covered by a different healthcare system. In
addition, we expect different forms of response biases (e.g., participation rates were
much higher in individuals with higher education levels). As a result, the cohort
cannot be taken as statistically representative. With these limitations in mind, its
participants are diverse and represent a range of ancestries, regional origins,
socioeconomic statuses, and environmental exposures.
This is outlined in the discussion:
participants with a range of ancestral backgrounds, CaG is not completely representative
of the province’s population. On average, CaG participants have higher education
attainment and income than the overall population. Furthermore, because recruitment took
place in six cities, several geographical regions of Quebec such as the Northwestern
Abitibi-Temiscamingue region are not well captured in the CaG dataset. Indigenous
residents are also not well represented in CaG.
We also have added context in the section on ancestry from the Americas, as this
context is important to interpret these results.
“The CaG cohort was recruited in the south of Quebec from individuals enrolled in the
provincial healthcare plan, both factors that likely led to reduced participation by
individuals with elevated ancestry from the Americas: many indigenous communities live
outside our sampling areas, and Indigenous people are more likely to be enrolled in a
federal rather than provincial healthcare plan.”
2.9) Compared to the original Quebec population comprising French, Canadian
(overlapping with French), British, Indigenous, Other European and Non-
European population needs to be discussed in regard to the current study
population. Also a chart as per timeline when these populations originated in
Quebec could be a good overall demonstration of the Quebec population with a
highlight of what is covered by the current study (sample collection centers). This
will provide a clear image of the studied population at present time, which might be
predominant at some time point in history.
Response: The CARTaGENE cohort is sampled from the present-day population of
Quebec which, as the Reviewer describes, is the result of multiple waves of migration.
The regions sampled include the largest metropolitan areas in the province, and as
such, are expected to represent most major ancestral groups present in the province,
subject to the biases highlighted in the text. A thorough description of the migration
history of Quebec is out of scope for this work. We do agree with the reviewer that
more context would help the reader unfamiliar with the history of the province to
situate the cohort in a broader context. We have therefore added a few lines in the
introduction pointing the reader to relevant resources describing this history and
added a timeline in Supplementary Figure 1 which summarizes the main
establishments and migration events in Quebec.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks on code availability):
The code could be added to a Github repository with comments (optional).
Response: We are committed to open science and reproducibility. As such, we have ensured
that the main source code used to process the data and generate data for tables and figures
is available through figshare at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28891670, as well as
being available in a Github repository. The figshare download includes the following sections:
 ARG-based imputation and regional frequency - contains source code used to
identify likely carriers in genotyping array data in the "Variants of clinical interest (VCI):
using CaG to go beyond founder variants" section of the manuscript.
8
 GWAS - contains source code used for genome-wide association scans, fine-
mapping, and generating tables and figures in the "Genome-wide association studies
(GWAS)" section of the manuscript.
 Genotype_processing - contains source code used for the genotyping array data pre-
processing before genotype imputation and GWASs.
 HLA - contains source code used for the HLA data generation, analysis and generating
tables and figures in the "HLA genotyping" section of the manuscript.
 IBD - contains source code used for the identity-by-descent (IBD) analyses and
generating tables and figures in the "Genetic structure in CaG" section of the
manuscript.
 Imputation - contains source code used for preparing and benchmarking the
genotype imputation reference panel in the "Haplotype reference panel and genotype
imputation " section of the manuscript.
 PCA_UMAP_clustering - contains source code used for the Principal Component
Analyses (PCA) and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) in the
"Genetic structure in CaG" section of the manuscript.
 Phasing - contains source code used for statistical phasing and benchmarking
phasing quality in the "Haplotype reference panel and genotype imputation" section
of the manuscript.
These files are also available in the following GitHub repositories:

manuscript tables and figures; data processing steps.
 https://github.com/CERC-Genomic-Medicine/WEGS_pipelines - for pipelines used
for the variant calling in benchmark WGS datasets.
